title: [Chapitre] III. Réseaux via découpages : notes manuscrites (08/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction: Context (pp. 12-14). The chapter aims to recover the structure of an ordered set L from purely combinatorial data on its finite subsets. The data are the 'découpages' or flags Drap_n(L) (finite subsets that are chains) and a betweenness relation. Order is defined branch by branch. On p. 12 Grothendieck fixes an 'origin' pair (a,b) with a<b and shows the order can be described by betweenness alone. L_{>=b}, L_{<=a} and ]a,b[ are expressed through betweenness. Then u<=v holds iff there exist x in L_{<=a} and y in L_{>=b} (so x<y) such that (a) u and v are between x and y, and (b) u is between x and v, or (c) v is between u and y. For the converse direction he needs the Lemma on this page. Lemma: let L be an ordered set and x, y, u, v elements ('trois' is a slip; there are four) such that (a) u, v are between x and y; (b) u is between x and v, or (c) v is between u and y (either one suffices); (d) x<y. Then x<=u<=v<=y. Proof: the hypotheses force I={x,y,u,v} to be a découpage, i.e. a chain. So one may assume L=I is a totally ordered set with 2, 3 or 4 elements. Several crossed-out attempts at a case analysis (taking x as the smallest element, supposing u<x, and so on) are abandoned. Final argument: since u, v are between x and y and x<y, we get x<=u,v<=y. Since u is between x and v, we get x<=u<=v. OK. NB: the proof used (1) a property of the order relation he calls 'distributivité', presumably that betweenness data make the four points lie on one branch; and (2) that L is filtering both upwards and downwards. Hypothesis (a) served only to deduce the relation 'a and b disjoint' from 'a is strictly between b and c'. This sets up p. 14: the order is reconstructed from Drap_2(L), the strict betweenness relation R(a,b,c), and the two filtrations. He then shows that R(a,b,c) can itself be recovered from Drap_3 and connected components of the sets C(ε). The whole page is an elementary step in an axiomatization of tree-like ordered sets via betweenness.
errors: 'trois éléments' should read 'quatre éléments' (x, y, u, v).
The reduction to a totally ordered I is asserted, not proved here. It depends on the branch structure ('distributivité', filtering hypotheses) mentioned only in the NB.
Hypothesis d) is written with a heavy symbol (<= or <), but the proof uses x<y. The degenerate case is harmless either way.

ideas.what: Reconstruction of an order relation (up to choice of an origin pair a<b) from a ternary betweenness relation on the branches of an ordered set
ideas.modern_name: betweenness relations / axiomatics of order; betweenness in trees and median structures
ideas.usually_credited_to: Pasch, Hilbert, Huntington (axioms of betweenness, ca. 1880-1924); Pitcher & Smiley 1942; later work on tree/median betweenness

ideas.what: Lemma: if u, v lie between x<y and u lies between x and v (or v between u and y), then x<=u<=v<=y, proved by reduction to a finite chain
ideas.modern_name: elementary betweenness lemma for linear orders

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine verification lemma in an elementary reconstruction of an order from betweenness and flag data. It is classical in content, and the only interest is as context for Grothendieck's 1986 'réseaux via découpages' programme.
transcription_corrections: 'trois éléments' is in the manuscript but is a slip for four elements.
'DPS' is Grothendieck's abbreviation, likely 'dès lors on peut supposer': 'on peut supposer L = I est un ens. tot. ordonné'.
The line after 'Dém' likely reads 'les conditions b) c) d) [impliquent] que I = {x,y,u,v} est un découpage' rather than 'ne font que'.
In the crossed-out passage, 'on aurait vous' is probably 'on aurait' followed by the struck-out 'v<u<x<y'.
Hypothesis d) may be 'x < y' (strict); the proof uses x<y.
